~/about
# AI builds fast. Someone senior decides what's good.
AI speeds up building enormously. It does not deliver a good product on its own. That takes vision, craft and hard choices, made by someone who has sat on the buyer's side of the table. That is the job here.
Talk to Nico How we ship
nico@meihuizen.ai: ~/about
$ whoami
Nico Meihuizen
founder · AI-native software engineer
$ history | head -1
age 12 · IBM 5110 · a terminal and a manual
$ cat career.log
2011–2025 enterprise IT sales · IBM · SoftLayer · Oracle · Minitab
2022 Minitab 100% Club
2026 meihuizen.ai · Kaunas
$ ls ./cs-degree
ls: cannot access './cs-degree': No such file or directory
$ ls ./shipped
second-audience/ agent-fritz/ five/ this-site/
~/who you get
## One person owns it. Start to finish.
Founder and AI-native software engineer, after fourteen years of enterprise sales. I own the architecture, the process and the hard technical calls, whether the team around it is me and nine agents or your own twenty engineers.
No agency layers, no junior handoffs, no account manager relaying your notes. You talk to the person who writes the code. Having been the account manager for fourteen years is exactly why.
// from an IBM 5110 to enterprise IT
I got my first computer at 12: an IBM 5110. No tutorials, just a terminal and a manual. Coding stayed a hobby through a career selling data center, cloud and SaaS to buyers who could smell a shallow pitch instantly.
That career taught one habit: know the product inside out before you present it. Now I build the product.
TypeScriptPythonReactNode.jsLLM toolingAgentic workflows
~/vision
## Your next buyer meets you through an agent.
It reads your site, compares you with three others and answers before anyone picks up the phone. It answers whether or not you gave it anything to answer with. Most companies have not noticed yet. The agent does not care.
Two things follow. Companies have to be readable by the machines that now do the first round of buying. And one senior person with agents has the reach a department used to need. We build for both: sites and data that agents get right, and agents that do real work.
What we sell, we run on ourselves first
✓ second-audience
Scanned this site first. It found things.
✓ agent-fritz
Does the inside sales on this site. You can try him now.
✓ five
Holds our own pipeline. It knows which deal went quiet.
~/what we're good at
## Four things, done properly.
{ }
### Agentic products
Multi-agent systems and LLM-driven tools, built with a process disciplined enough that faster also means reliable.
see: Agent Fritz →
→→
### Automated AI workflows
Agent-driven pipelines that take the repetitive work off your team, with a human sign-off where it matters.
see: Second Audience →
[ ]
### Local-first, privacy-first
Software that runs on your own hardware, so your data stays yours. Built in the EU, for the GDPR you actually live with.
see: One Acre, Zero Dependency →
</>
### Full-stack web platforms
Architecture, design, deployment and upkeep. This site is written for people and for machines, in English and Lithuanian.
see: this site →
~/how we ship
## Fast, with the brakes still on.
Speed from AI is only worth something if the process catches what AI gets wrong. So every change runs the same route, whether it is a typo or a new agent. No exceptions for "small" ones.
● pipeline · branch → main✓ all checks passed · deployed
- branchEvery change on its own branch. Main is never edited directly.
- pull requestDescribed, linked to the why, readable a year later.
- ci: scan + testsCodeQL security scan and unit tests on every push and pull request.
- ci: evalsFritz answers his trap questions on every preview deploy. Red means no merge.
- human reviewNico reads the diff. Nothing merges unread.
- cd: deployMerge to main ships it. No hand-copied files.
- monitorPublic status page. If it breaks, you see it too.
CodeQL · this sitenpm test · agent-fritz-guardrails, every pushFritz evals · every Vercel deployESLint + Next.js build · Fivesite diagnostics · SEO and security sweep
git
Everything in version control
Code, prompts, evals and site copy. If it is not in Git, it does not exist.
ci/cd
Green checks or no release
A red check on a preview means it does not merge. Nobody overrides it to make a deadline.
evals
Agents are tested like code
A fixed set of trap questions every agent has to pass before a change goes out.
secrets
Keys never touch the repo
Credentials live in the hosting platform's settings, per environment.
gdpr
EU data, written down
A privacy page that says what is kept, how long, and who to ask to delete it.
open
Proof in public
Fritz's guardrails and test harness are a public repo. Read the tests yourself.
~/how I work with AI
## A tool. A very good one.
01
It is a tool, not the workA model on its own produces nothing a client can use. The result comes from the workflow around it.
02
Pipelines beat promptsOne prompt is a gamble. Controlled inputs and repeatable steps are a production method.
03
Default output is a draftIt ships when it survives review, not when it compiles.
04
Know where it breaksEvery model fails somewhere. Knowing where decides whether AI is the right tool at all.
05
The model does not decide what is goodIt widens what one person can build. The judgement stays human.
~/the crew
## One human. Nine agents. One dog.
You don't need thirty employees any more. One person with agents has the reach that used to take a department. Pretending otherwise is the old org chart with better marketing.
The one who steers
Nico
thinks, decides, verifies, and signs it
The one who fetches
Fritz, the dog
brings back only what is actually there. The agent got that rule from him.

Kimilong context, and curiosity

BigMLpredictive models, and new here
Agent Fritzanswers from these pages only, and fetches the leads
Tool names say which tools. No affiliation, partnership or endorsement implied.
~/the mobile lab
## The office has wheels.
There is no office to visit, on purpose. The work happens where the work is: at your table, on a call, or in the van parked outside. It runs fully off grid, so a discovery day in your car park and a build sprint in a Lithuanian forest run on the same power, the same uplink and the same coffee machine.
Anywhere in the EU, at your door within 48 hours.

I changed my mind for three reasons. An MB costs almost nothing to hold open. VAT and an entity turned out to be the price of entry to the conversations I want, not the reward for winning them. And Second Audience stopped being an idea.
A page that was never wrong is a page nobody ever edited.

pages.title: meihuizen.ai | Privacy, Every Flow Named
pages.description: How meihuizen.ai handles personal data: every flow, processor and retention period, analytics only with consent, and how to reach us about your data.
pages.text:
meihuizen.ai
~/privacy
# What happens to your data here, every flow named.
Most privacy pages are written to be skipped. This one is written to be checked: every place your data comes in, where it goes, who processes it and how long it stays. If something on this site does not match this page, this page is wrong, and we want to hear it.
~/short-version
analytics
Google Analytics loads only after you click "Accept". Until then nothing from Google loads and no analytics cookie is set.
fonts
Served from this site. No request to Google Fonts.
agent fritz
Your conversation is processed to answer you, not stored. The server keeps counts, not content, unless you send a request.
requests
What you type into a scan or contact form reaches our mailbox and stays there for six months, unless it turns into a working relationship.
never
No advertising cookies, no selling or sharing of data, no profiling.
~/who-we-are
controller
MB Meihuizen AI (Mažoji bendrija Meihuizen AI), company code 308157412, Laisvės al. 110, LT-44253 Kaunas, Lithuania.
privacy contact
dpo@meihuizen.ai for every request about your data: access, correction, deletion, objection. General questions: info@meihuizen.ai.
scope
This page covers meihuizen.ai, Agent Fritz on this site, the contact form and Second Audience scans. Five, our sales app, gets its own privacy notice before it takes paying customers.
~/every-flow
One row per flow: what is collected, where it goes, how long it stays, and why we are allowed to.
visiting a page
Your IP address, browser and the page you ask for reach GitHub Pages, which hosts the site and keeps server logs under its own terms.basis: legitimate interest (running and securing the site)
your choices
Your light/dark theme and your cookie choice are stored in your own browser (localStorage). They never leave your device.basis: needed for what you asked for
analytics
Only after "Accept": Google Analytics 4 sets _ga cookies and sends page views to Google. IP addresses are not logged or stored by Google Analytics 4. Google keeps the data for [check: retention period set in the GA4 property]. Change your mind any time: . A later reject deletes the cookies.basis: your consent
agent fritz
Each question and the conversation so far go to our function on Vercel, region Frankfurt, and from there to the Anthropic API (model Claude Haiku) to write the answer. Our server logs counts (language, page, timing), never the text. Anthropic deletes API inputs and outputs within 30 days, or keeps them up to 2 years if its safety systems flag a conversation. The conversation itself lives in your browser tab (sessionStorage) and is gone when you close it. Your IP address is held briefly in memory to limit abuse and is never written anywhere.basis: legitimate interest (answering the question you asked)
scan and contact requests
What you type (name, company, email, phone, domain) and the chat that led to it are emailed to our mailbox at Proton, and you get a confirmation email. A short version (your details, your first question, the page you were on and your local time) also goes to Nico's phone as a Telegram message, so he sees it straight away. We keep both for six months. If it turns into a working relationship, it becomes part of that and is kept as long as the relationship needs.basis: steps you asked for before a contract
live chat with nico
If Agent Fritz offers to bring Nico into the chat and you say yes, Nico gets a Telegram message with the last few messages of your chat. While he is in, what you type goes to his phone through Telegram, and what he types comes back to you. The messages are held in our store (Upstash, region Frankfurt) only while the chat lasts and are deleted automatically within a day; the Telegram copies follow the same rule as other requests.basis: steps you asked for before a contract
contact form
Name, email and message are sent through a Vercel function to our Proton mailbox. Kept for six months, same rule as above.basis: legitimate interest (answering you)
second audience scan
The scan reads your public web pages, which is business content, not personal data. After a free scan we keep only the report and delete the raw captures. For paying clients we keep the raw captures for as long as the engagement needs them for re-scans.basis: steps you asked for before a contract, then the contract
booking a call
If Agent Fritz books a call for you, your name, email address and the time go into Nico's Google Calendar (Google Workspace), which sends you the invite with a Google Meet link. Nico's phone gets a short Telegram message about it, as with other requests. The appointment stays in the calendar as the record of the call.basis: steps you asked for before a contract
~/processors
Every company that processes personal data for this site, and where.
GitHub
Hosting (GitHub Pages). GitHub Inc., United States.
Vercel
Functions for Agent Fritz and the contact form, run in Frankfurt. Vercel Inc., United States.
Anthropic
The model behind Agent Fritz. Anthropic PBC, United States.
Proton
Email. Proton AG, Switzerland.
Upstash
Short-lived storage for live chats with Nico, deleted within a day. Upstash Inc., United States; data stored in Frankfurt (EU).
Telegram
Notifications of scan and contact requests, and live chats, on Nico's phone. Telegram Messenger Inc., British Virgin Islands; for accounts registered in the EEA, Telegram stores the data in the Netherlands.
Google

pages.description: A sales agent for your website: answers only from your pages, books meetings, qualifies leads and hands over documents. Try it: it sits in the corner of this page.
pages.text:
open the repo
# Agent Fritz
The chat in the corner of this page is the product. Ask it anything about meihuizen.ai: it reads the pages it needs, answers from what they say, shows you which ones, and says so when something is not on the site. Named after Nico's dog, who also only brings back what is actually there.
On this site Fritz is configured as a sales assistant: it qualifies leads and takes on real pre-sales and inside sales work. That is our version. Fritz can be whatever your business needs, a customer care rep, a doctor's assistant, a support desk: buy it as it is, or have it built around your regulatory requirements.
Reads before it answersFritz gets an index of the site, not the site. To say anything it has to open the page, and the page it opened is listed under the answer.
Not on the site is an answerAsked for something no page says, it says that, and gives the email address. No estimate, no plausible filler.
Nothing goes out unconfirmedDetails read back, the visitor says yes, then it acts. The server refuses anything the visitor did not type.
## // in action
Real conversations in the window you are looking at. Tap a picture to see it full size.
Every answer names its source. Tap “where does it say so?” and the exact sentence appears.
Not published is an answer. The VAT number has not been issued yet, so Fritz says exactly that.
Ask for a product sheet, get the PDF.
Real free times from Nico's calendar, in the visitor's own time.
Read back, confirmed, booked. The invite with a Meet link goes out.
One anonymised case as proof, then the free scan offer.
Nico in the chat, handing Fritz a task from his phone.
Nico's phone: the qualified lead, the ring, every line of the chat.
## // overview
## Why most website chatbots are a liability
A chatbot that answers from a model's general knowledge fills gaps with something plausible. Under your logo, a plausible wrong price or an invented company detail is your mistake, not the model's. This site keeps a dated correction for exactly that kind of claim on its credentials page: a legal entity stated as fact before it existed.
## What Fritz does
- Answers from your pages, in the visitor's language and in the formal register your site uses, with the source under every answer.
- Hands over documents. Ask for a product sheet and it is there as a download. Ask for one that does not exist and it says so, and offers to have someone send it.
- Books the meeting. It offers real free times from the calendar, reads the details back and sends the invite with a video link. Intro calls, demos and longer meetings.
- Passes leads on. The visitor's question, contact details and the whole conversation land in the inbox, with one line on what the visitor said about their situation: the pain, who decides, the timeline.
- Knows the time. Outside office hours it says so, names the moment someone is back, and before a weekend asks whether it can wait.
- Brings a human in. When Nico is available, Fritz asks the visitor whether they want him in the chat and rings his phone. Nico joins the same conversation.
- Takes instructions in that conversation. With Nico in the chat, he can hand Fritz a task from his phone ("plan a 30-minute demo next week", "share the product sheet"). Fritz does it and gives the conversation back. Only Nico can; a visitor typing the same words gets nowhere.
- Feeds Five, as an option. Leads Fritz qualifies can land in Five as FQLs, Fritz Qualified Leads: in an incoming queue, not in your five slots. Fritz qualifies; you decide what gets a slot.
## How it sells
Fritz works the way a good inside sales rep works, with three methods. SPIN to ask the one question that shows a visitor what a problem costs them. Challenger to correct a belief with a fact from the site rather than an argument. MEDDPICC to notice who decides and when, so the lead that reaches you is already qualified. The methods decide what it asks. They never decide what it claims: every fact still comes from a page.
## Guardrails that live on the server
A prompt is a request. These are rules the server enforces, whatever the model says:
- No email address, phone number or domain is used unless the visitor typed it, and nothing is sent until it has been read back and confirmed.
- An address on a domain that does not exist or takes no mail goes back to the visitor to check, before it reaches you as a lead that bounces.
- A phone number that is not on the site never reaches the screen.
- Only the site owner can give Fritz instructions, and only from his own phone.
## Tested with traps
A fixed set of questions runs against Fritz before a change ships, and the traps are the point: the VAT number that has not been issued yet, the LLC that never existed, the team of engineers that is one person, the case company it must not name. A wrong answer on a trap means the change does not go out. Test runs send nothing, book nothing and ring no one.
## What you get on your site
The same build, pointed at your pages. The knowledge is rebuilt from your content, so editing a page and changing what the agent knows are one change. Your languages, answering in the visitor's. The actions wired to your inbox, your calendar and your systems. A test set written for the traps in your business. A spend cap, per-visitor limits, and a switch that turns it off without a deploy. The function runs in Frankfurt and conversations are not logged: the server keeps counts, not content, except the conversation a visitor sends as a request.
## What it costs
Fritz is a custom build, not a wrapper around a chatbot. Getting it right for a business takes time: your content, your languages, your actions, your traps, tested before anything ships. The price follows that work: how many pages, how many languages, which actions it takes. Starting from a Second Audience scan, it is priced on the value the scan shows. Without one, tell Nico what your site covers and he will work out a price with you. We ship AI plus a human: Nico builds it, tests it and stays on it.
## Status
Live on this site since September 2026, answering every visitor in their own language. No client deployment yet: this site is the first, and the one you can test hardest.

pages.title: Off-Grid AI Homestead | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: Off-grid AI farming on two plots 2,256 km apart: Prora on the German Baltic in summer, Castelo Branco in Portugal in winter. Solar Pico node, DWD history.
pages.text:
open the repo
# One Acre, Zero Dependency
Off-grid, AI-driven farming on two plots 2,256 km apart: Prora through summer, Castelo Branco through winter.
A solar-powered field module (Birdbox) collects soil and local weather data. Through the Open-Meteo historical archive API (2006-2026) we bring in twenty years of regional weather history. Eurostat Agriculture Statistics adds regional yield figures, coarse ones though: annual, per hectare and per region, not per bed. The Thun calendar supplies a planting and harvesting calendar based on the position of the moon. This project computes it correctly and tests it, instead of assuming it.
The calculations run in Python. A locally running model (ML/LLM) lays the results side by side and predicts which vegetables and crops give the best yield per planting, when to sow them, and which rotations work best on a small field of 4,000 m².
The aim of this project is to give farmers, hobby growers and families something to hold on to, so they can grow organically at small and large scale, responsibly and successfully, on modern technique and age-old concepts that protect the earth.
status: phase 0. Nothing is built yet. The plan is.
From sensor to scheduler. Storage is the seam.
Two plots, one seasonProra runs through the summer, Castelo Branco through the winter. Between them there is never a month with nothing growing.
Nothing leaves the acreSun to sensor to laptop to schedule. The model runs locally, which is the only way the off-grid claim survives contact with a bill.
The model proposes, Python disposesEvery suggestion passes a deterministic rule set before it becomes a task. What fails the rules is dropped, and the drop is logged.
## // overview
## The question
How much of a small farm's daily decision-making can genuinely off-grid AI handle end to end, from sensor to scheduler?
That is the whole project. Two plots on opposite sides of Europe, worked in alternation, documented publicly through 2026 and 2027. The full write-up, the ADRs and the data sources are in the repo.
## // stack
Pico 2 WMicroPythonPython 3.11SQLiteskyfieldLSTMOllamaBLE / LoRaDWD / IPMAERA5-Land
### AI-Homestead
The repo. Build plan, ADRs, data sources, and the figures on this page.
CODE
### Project overview
Short brief. The two plots, the three commitments, and what each data source can and cannot claim.
PDF
## // where
## Two plots, 2,256 km apart
14.6 degrees of latitude apart. You follow the growing season instead of fighting it.
### Prora summer
WhereRügen, German Baltic coast
Latitude54.39 °N
ReferenceDWD Arkona, station 00183, 33 km north
Winter solstice7.0 h of daylight, sun peaks at 12.2 °
### Castelo Branco winter
WhereCentral Portugal, inland
Latitude39.82 °N
ReferenceIPMA long series, plus ERA5-Land
Winter solstice9.2 h of daylight, sun peaks at 26.7 °
## // commitments
## Three things this project does not compromise on
- 1 · Off-grid means off-grid. No cloud LLM in the daily loop.
- 2 · Every number carries its provenance and its error bars. A €30 sensor claiming ±0.3 pH does not get to report pH to one decimal.
- 3 · The biodynamic calendar is a hypothesis under test, not a scheduling rule.
## // the field node
## A Pico, not a Pi
Prora gets 7.0 hours of daylight at the solstice, sun at 12.2 degrees. That is what the node is sized for.
A duty-cycled Pico runs on roughly sixty times less than an always-on Pi.
Two failure modes kill the node sooner than any sensor: condensation, and charging below zero.
Under 20 metres BLE, above that LoRa. The ingest layer makes that a one-module change.
## // data
## Two plots, two weather services
Prora leans on DWD Arkona, 33 km away, with measured radiation from 1947. Castelo Branco has no equivalent open history and leans on ERA5-Land. That asymmetry is not papered over.
## // the calendar
## The Thun calendar, honestly implemented
Computed from the ephemeris in thirty-minute steps. Sidereal, not tropical.
Tropical signs sit 24 to 25 degrees off the real constellations. Get this wrong and every day type is wrong.
Real IAU boundaries are unequal, so 2027 comes out at 107 root days against 67 flower days.
Ascending and descending is a 27.3-day cycle, entirely separate from waxing and waning at 29.53.
The evidence does not support the trigon effect. The calendar is therefore logged as a covariate and tested, never used as a rule.
## // models
## The LLM proposes, Python disposes
Every number is computed in tested Python. The model selects, prioritises and explains, and returns JSON validated against a schema. What it is aimed at: yield per square metre.
## // roadmap
## Ten phases
September 2026 to October 2027. Every phase has a done-when you can actually check.
MIT for the code. Weather data from DWD (CC BY 4.0), IPMA, and Open-Meteo (CC-BY-4.0). Ephemerides from JPL via skyfield. No copyrighted calendar data is redistributed.
© 2026 Nico Meihuizen02 / 02

pages.title: Second Audience cases: what AI agents got wrong | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: Six anonymised Second Audience scans: what AI agents said about real companies, which page on their own site explained it, and the fix.
pages.text:
# What the agents said
Six real Second Audience scans, with every name taken out. In each one we asked AI agents the questions a buyer asks, then traced every answer back to the page on the company's own site that explains it.
The agent answers are illustration. The finding is always text on the company's own pages, which anyone can open and check.
## // how to read these
## Real scans, no names
Every case on this page is a free scan of a real company's public website, run in August 2026. We do not name the companies, and we do not confirm or deny a guess. Sectors are described one level up, and prices, dates and figures that could be searched for are left out.
Clients who went on to buy are never published here, not even anonymised. What they paid for stays theirs.
## // case 01 · expert network
## The client case that did not exist
What we found. A network of independent consultants selling expertise to corporate clients. Its only client case page was a template that was never filled in, still listed in its own sitemap. Its client logos were images with no text beside them. Its commercial model was published nowhere, and its registered address appeared only in the privacy statement.
What the agents did.
- Asked what the company had actually delivered, every agent produced something different. One invented a full case at a real bank, with challenge, approach and result, and named the company as the source three times.
- Not one of sixteen answers named any of the real clients whose logos were on the site.
- One agent worked out a per-day margin split between client, consultant and company, with no source at all.
- Asked where the company is based, one agent in four was right.
What was working. The service pages were plain text, and all four agents described the services correctly. Key figures written as text came back right every time.
The fix. Real cases with a number, one line of text beside each logo, the legal identity on the contact page, and the template page out of the sitemap. No rebuild.
The lesson. An agent that finds nothing rarely says nothing. It fills the gap, and it puts your name under what it filled in.
## // case 02 · regulated asset manager
## The old press release that won
What we found. A registered fund manager selling a credit fund. Its investment criteria existed twice: on the current strategy page, and inside a press release from several years earlier that was still live and indexed. Neither said which one was current. Who may invest, from what amount and for how long was published nowhere. The site also refused automated retrieval, so every agent worked from stored search fragments, which carry no date.
What the agents did.
- Three of five agents quoted the old criteria as current. One gave both versions on the same day, in two different answers, both labelled as the company's own.
- All five supplied an entry threshold the company never published.
- Two turned it into portfolio advice: a percentage of the reader's investable assets to put into the fund.
- One quoted a statutory warning in the company's name that appears nowhere on its site.
What was working. Everything stated once, in plain text, on a current page travelled accurately. All five agents kept the exact supervisory wording and the sustainability disclosures, the paragraphs a summary usually drops.
The fix. One dated line on the old press release pointing to the current page, one approved qualifying paragraph on the pages that carry the fund claims, and the retrieval block reviewed.
The lesson. When the same fact lives twice on your domain, the agent has to choose, and nothing tells it which one is current. When a regulated fact lives nowhere, something else fills it in, under your name.
## // case 03 · consumer brand
## Four values for one health-sensitive fact
What we found. An international consumer brand with market sites in many countries. One product's key figure was published four different ways across the brand's own market pages, three of them on a single page. A reassurance about a medically sensitive situation appeared in three languages, while another market page on the same domain told the reader to consult a doctor. An allergen statement was answered three incompatible ways. The contact pages offered forms only.
What the agents did.
- Given the simplest possible question, three agents produced three different reconciliations of the conflicting figures. One invented a tolerance range that appears on no page anywhere.
- Asked in sloppy, real-world phrasing by someone about to drive, two of three stated flatly that the product contained none at all, and one invented a rule in a regulator's name.
- One agent did every step correctly and still told a reader in a sensitive situation that the product was completely safe, by quoting the brand's page for another market and translating it.
What was working. The one fact written once, with a number and the threshold it is measured against, held in every phrasing, at every agent, in every run. The brand's other products carried one consistent figure everywhere.
What we got wrong. We predicted the agents would hide the contradiction. They did not hide it. They resolved it, and the resolution was the damage.
The fix. One decision per fact per market, written once, and the same figure in a structured product record so no machine has to choose.
The lesson. Agents do not stay silent about a contradiction. They reconcile it and state the result as confidently as a fact. The sloppier the question, the more absolute the answer.
## // case 04 · retail bank
## The emergency number that held
What we found. We did not test what this bank sells. We tested the number someone calls when their card has just been stolen. The emergency-line page was built properly and delivered its text on the first request. The general customer service page did not mention the emergency line, and delivered no readable text on the first request. The two numbers differ only in their last digits and circulate in several spellings.
What the agents did.
- Asked for the emergency number, the agents were right eleven times out of twelve, including a mangled brand name and a five-word panic fragment. The best result we have measured on a question that matters.
- Three of four agents took the bank's phone numbers from its press site rather than its service pages, because the press site delivered text.
- Asked the ordinary question about the customer service number, one agent built its own emergency route and sent a stolen card to the general line.
- After a one-letter typo, one agent answered for a different bank entirely. That is agent behaviour, not a site defect, and we reported it as such.
What was working. The emergency route itself. The page built properly wins, and the bank already owns the proof of the fix.
What we got wrong. Four of our six predictions. We expected answers to get gradually worse as the phrasing got sloppier. They do not. It is a cliff, not a dial, and nobody can predict which phrasing goes over it.
The fix. One sentence naming the emergency line at the top of the customer service page, in text that arrives on the first request. That is the whole finding.
The lesson. The page that is built properly wins. The pages that are not lose to directories and press releases, even for your own phone number.
## // case 05 · online education provider
## One programme, three live offers
What we found. A high-priced online training programme with a money-back style guarantee. The same programme was live at three addresses, all three in the sitemap, with two prices, three durations and two different guarantee windows between them. The guarantee on the marketing page and in the binding agreement set different obligations. The headline outcome figure appeared with four different values, none with a year or a group size, and the current outcomes report was a PDF with no machine-readable text.
What the agents did.
- One agent sent the buyer to the oldest of the three pages, with the shorter guarantee and the lower price. Its citation was correct, because that text really is there.
- The same agent gave two different prices on the same day. The only difference was how the question was typed.
- One agent read both guarantee texts and told the buyer, unprompted, to check with the company before paying.
- One agent quoted an outcome figure in quotation marks with the exact address of the company's own report. The figure is not in that report's readable text.
What was working. The binding agreement was the best-built page on the domain. Every agent reached it, quoted it correctly, and told the buyer to rely on it.
The fix. One programme page with the other versions made canonical or taken out of the sitemap, the binding conditions stated on the marketing page, and the outcome figures as plain text with year and group size.
The lesson. An old version that stays live and stays in the sitemap is not an archive. It is a second offer.
## // case 06 · private bank
## The founding year in the page title
What we found. A long-established private bank. The page title, and the title shown when the page is shared, carried a founding year decades earlier than the bank's own timeline and homepage text. The earlier year belonged to the founding family's previous business, not to the bank.
What was working. Everywhere except the title, the bank told one consistent story.
The fix. One title, matching the timeline.
The lesson. A person reading both understands at once. A machine that carries the title away makes the bank decades older, with the bank as the source.
## // the pattern
## What the six have in common
- Text arrives, everything else gets filled in. Plain text on a current page travelled accurately in every case. Images, templates, PDFs without text and facts published nowhere were filled in by the agent or by someone else.
- The second answer is the engine. In most scans the strongest finding came from the same fact appearing twice on the company's own domain, worded differently.
- Agents reconcile, they do not stay silent. Faced with a contradiction, they invent a range, a structure or a rule, and state it with full confidence.
- The source label carries your name. The reader does not see a machine's guess. They see what looks like your own claim.
- It is rarely a rebuild. In almost every case the biggest fix was a sentence, a canonical tag, a sitemap clean-up or a dated note on an old page.
## We print our misses
Before asking a single agent, we write down what we expect. Across these scans we were wrong about half the time, and every miss is in the report with the reason. A report that shows only the hits is a sales document and gets read as one.
## // your own site
## Would any of this be true for you?
The free scan runs the same steps on your own domain and shows you what came out, with the page that explains each answer.
© 2026 Nico Meihuizen05 / 06

pages.title: Second Audience: AI Agent Website Scan | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: A recurring audit that measures what AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity can actually read, do, and get wrong on your website.
pages.text:
# Second Audience
Your website has two kinds of visitor now. One has eyes. The other is agentic AI: it never runs your JavaScript, reads only what your server sends, and then answers questions about you for its visitors, who never open your page. Second Audience measures what that second visitor can actually do.
A service, not a tool. The scan is run by a person and a model working the same case, because the claim being sold is that machines read confidently and get facts wrong, and that is not a claim a machine can certify about itself.
Fetched twiceThe same page with JavaScript and without. What disappears is what a non-rendering crawler never sees.
One fact, four answersA price published once, in a form that invites filling in the rest. Four agents, four numbers, one of them right.
Predictions written firstEighteen written down before an agent was asked anything. Nine of them wrong, and that is in the report.
## // overview
## Seven steps, in this order, and the agents come last
The order is the product. A scan that starts at the agents finds technical imperfections and no money. Every strong finding this year came out of step three: does the same fact appear somewhere else on the domain, worded differently. An FAQ, a stale translation, an orphan page, a press release from four years ago.
## What a finding looks like
An expert network had one client case page, and it was a template that was never filled in. Asked what the company had actually delivered, four agents gave four different answers. One invented a full case at a real bank and named the company as the source three times.
An education provider had the same programme live at three addresses, each with a different price, duration or guarantee. One agent sent the buyer to the oldest page, with the shorter guarantee. Its citation was correct, because that text really is there.
Every example on this site is anonymised: no names, no figures that can be searched for, and we do not confirm guesses. Six cases are written up in full on the cases page. > six cases
## We publish our own misses
Eighteen predictions written down before a single agent was asked. Nine of them wrong. That is in the report, with the reason. A report that shows only the hits is a sales document and gets read as one.
## A person and a model, working the same case
The machine does the volume: every page fetched twice and compared, every business fact diffed against every other instance of itself on the domain, every cited document opened to see whether its text layer holds what the citation claims. A person makes the three decisions no loop produces: which object carries the revenue, which fact is worth chasing, and whether a citation actually holds. Both are wrong regularly. Each has to answer to the other before anything ships.
## It does not stay fixed
Engines update, pages change, and a claim you have removed keeps being answered for months afterwards. There is a dated measurement of exactly that on this domain. So the work repeats: the same prompts at one week, one month and three months, against the same pages.
## What it costs
The free scan is free. What comes after is priced on the complexity of your site, and every scan report comes with prices for three routes:
- 1 · Do it yourself. Use the implementation report and implement the findings yourself.
- 2 · Full implementation. We handle the complete implementation, including monitoring and the re-scans at one week, one month and three months.
- 3 · Implementation + Agent Fritz. The full implementation, bundled with Agent Fritz on your site, answering visitors from your corrected pages.
With a scan, Fritz is priced on the value the scan shows.
## Status
Some free scans became paying clients. Their work is never published here, not even anonymised. Reports ship in Dutch and English, with a two-page annex on scope, data, rights and GDPR attached to every one.

pages.text:
# Portfolio Website
Not for sale: this is our showcase. What it shows is not the design but the structure: a site built to be read correctly by people and by the AI agents that now answer questions about it.
A terminal, not a templateTraffic lights, a mono path label, a card on a dark ground. The interface states what the site is about before a word is read.
Small behaviours, fenced inThe page is static. A handful of enclosed islands do the interactive work, each one small enough to reason about on its own.
A policy that refuses by defaultOutbound requests are blocked unless the policy names the destination. Security here is a feature of the page, not a header someone remembered.
## // overview
## Not the design. The second audience.
A good designer can make any site look right. That is the half people see. The other half is what an agent reads when someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity about you: which facts are there, how plainly they are stated, whether they can be misread. Most sites only paid for the first half. This one is built for both: facts stated plainly in English and Lithuanian, structured data that says the same thing as the page, and a credentials page that replaces the stale claims still in circulation.
## Try it
Ask ChatGPT what meihuizen.ai does and who is behind it. Then ask the same about your own company, and compare. Where the agents get us wrong, we say so: our misses are published on the Second Audience page.
## Want this for your site?
The site is not for sale. The approach is. Tell Nico what your site has to get right, for both audiences, and he will get back to you. Or ask Agent Fritz in the corner; he'll pass it on.
## Terminal-inspired portfolio interface
The site presents professional background, selected work, contact information, and project documentation in a focused terminal-inspired interface. The homepage includes a session-aware type sequence, responsive project cards, and direct navigation to the active work.
## Small JavaScript behaviors with clear boundaries
Vanilla JavaScript powers the typing sequence, form validation, responsive project lightboxes, image cleanup, keyboard dismissal, and body-scroll locking. Shared behavior lives in external same-origin scripts rather than being duplicated across pages.
## Security best practices as a feature
Every page carries a restrictive Content Security Policy as a meta tag, because GitHub Pages sends no custom headers. The only third-party script is Google Analytics. The site avoids unsafe HTML construction, and the contact form validates input, rejects honeypot submissions and sends through a rate-limited serverless function.
## Responsive, accessible presentation
Semantic headings, descriptive image alternatives, keyboard-friendly lightboxes, visible focus states, mobile touch targets, and CSS-centered image crops keep the experience usable across screen sizes.
